Zeus. The king of the Olympian gods and the supreme deity in Greek mythology, ruling over the sky, weather, justice, law, and cosmic order. He overthrew his father Cronus in the Titanomachy to establish Olympian rule, and his seat on Mount Olympus became the political and cosmic center of the divine realm. Known equally for his thunderous authority and his insatiable appetite for seduction, transforming himself into countless forms to pursue gods and mortals alike, Zeus embodies both the majesty of natural power and the capriciousness of desire. His extensive family tree of divine and heroic children forms the genealogical backbone of Greek mythology.

Zeus and his siblings were swallowed at birth by their father, the Titan Cronus, who feared a prophecy that his children would overthrow him. His mother Rhea saved Zeus by wrapping a stone in swaddling clothes, which Cronus swallowed instead. Zeus was hidden in a cave on Crete. When he came of age, Zeus forced Cronus to regurgitate his siblings, then led them in the Titanomachy, a ten-year war against the Titans that established Olympian supremacy. After defeating the Titans, Zeus drew lots with his brothers Poseidon and Hades to divide the cosmos. He won the sky and rule over all gods and mortals.

His signature weapon is the thunderbolt, forged for him by the Cyclopes, which he uses to punish mortals and gods alike. He defeated Typhon, the last monstrous challenge to his rule, a gargantuan serpent spawned by Gaia, and imprisoned the creature beneath Mount Etna, where its fire and writhing cause volcanic activity. His sacred animal is the eagle, and his sacred tree is the oak. His primary oracle was at Dodona, where priests interpreted divine will through the rustling of oak leaves. He is typically depicted wielding the thunderbolt and seated regally on a throne, sometimes with his eagle nearby.

Zeus frequently transformed himself to seduce both goddesses and mortals. He became a swan to seduce Leda, a white bull for Europa, a shower of gold for Danaë, and took countless other forms. His union with the mortal Alcmene, while disguised as her husband Amphitryon, produced Heracles, his most famous heroic son. His seductions sired divine and heroic offspring who became major figures. Athena, the goddess of wisdom, was born directly from his head. Apollo and Artemis are god and goddess of the sun and moon. Hermes is the messenger god, and Dionysus is the god of wine.

Zeus upholds Themis, or divine order, and Dike, or justice, punishing oath-breakers and enforcing moral codes. Mortals who violate guest-friendship or hospitality face his wrath. He is the patron of suppliants and the protector of family bonds, yet his own marriages and affairs are sources of conflict, particularly with his jealous wife Hera. Zeus represents the archetypal supreme god in Indo-European mythologies, a figure whose dominance, achieved through violence and maintained through force, reflects ancient power structures and the Greek fascination with the relationship between authority and arbitrariness.
